# What this book establishes {.unnumbered}

This book reports a research program on **surrogates for steady,
boundary-driven, three-dimensional PDE problems**: given a discretized
boundary (a surface mesh with normals and areas) and a few global conditions
such as the freestream direction, predict the fields on that boundary and in
the volume around it. The program built an architecture, ISLA (Invariant Slice Attention; the code class is `ISLA`, formerly `MeshTransformer2`),^[Pronounced "eye-la"; an *isla* is an island, a shape defined entirely by
its boundary. An earlier exact-kernel design of this program is documented in
the repository's `book/archive/` directory, outside this book.] and measured it
against the strongest available mainstream baseline, GeoTransolver, under one
frozen, parameter- and token-matched protocol on two production aerodynamics
datasets (DrivAerML, HiLiftAeroML), with a third (SHIFT-SUV) as a zero-shot
transfer target. The
audience is applied mathematicians and machine-learning researchers; every
term is defined at first use and every number is computed live from a
checked-in artifact.

## The result in one paragraph

**ISLA**, an SE(3)-equivariant soft-slice transformer, is **2.8x more accurate than GeoTransolver and
than plain Transolver when trained on 35 high-lift wing cases**, 1.3–2.2x more
accurate at 210 cases depending on the baseline, and at parity at 1,260
cases. The advantage holds on every one of the 180 shared validation cases at
35 cases, at every angle of attack including one absent from training, on
geometries never seen in training, and after every steel-man control we could
construct for the baselines (higher learning rate, doubled epochs, the same
attention family without a geometry encoder); a third seed reproduces it. In
engineering terms, from 35 CFD runs ISLA predicts lift and drag coefficients of
unseen configurations to about 3%, where the baselines reach 8–17%; at a
fixed angle of attack, 126 geometries give ISLA lift to 0.6% and a 5.0x
advantage over GeoTransolver on 18 never-seen geometries. It does
not transfer to DrivAerML, where the freestream is fixed: there GeoTransolver
is 1.2–1.3x more accurate than ISLA from 27 training cases up. At full data the
two architectures are at parity on HiLiftAeroML (GeoTransolver/ISLA = 1.02) and
ISLA is 8.5% behind on DrivAerML; ISLA trains stably across a learning-rate
decade where GeoTransolver degrades 4–14x; with its similarity gauge on it is
the most sampling-density-robust model measured (1.20x under a 10:1 density
bias against GeoTransolver's 3.6x), though that configuration is not the one
behind the accuracy numbers and the constant-gauge configuration degrades
13–14.5x; it is exactly rotation- and translation-covariant by construction;
and its peak training memory at 10,000 tokens is 1.5 GB, against
GeoTransolver's 4.6 GB.
On the interior, one architecture now covers both tasks: ISLA with its
interior queries admitted as interacting tokens matches GeoTransolver's
volume configuration on interior pressure (0.064 against 0.062) at 8.9M
parameters against 27.6M and without the signed-distance input that
GeoTransolver receives, trailing on velocity (1.16x) and eddy viscosity
(1.71x); at 54 training cars GeoTransolver leads it by 1.2x, as it leads
ISLA on the DrivAerML surface below full data. ISLA's passive,
query-independent decode from the surface sample alone is 2.6x behind on
pressure, the price of that contract. Where nothing leads is regime extrapolation: across an
angle-of-attack or stall boundary every architecture tested loses about a
factor of ten, so coverage, not architecture, governs that axis.

## The result in one picture

```{python}
#| label: fig-headline
#| fig-cap: >
#|   Data efficiency on HiLiftAeroML. Surface-pressure relative L2 error on
#|   the shared 180-case validation set versus number of training cases, for
#|   GeoTransolver (red circles), ISLA (blue squares) and plain
#|   Transolver (grey triangles, dashed). Lines join seed means; bands span
#|   the seeds; annotated factors are each baseline's error divided by ISLA's
#|   at the same rung (above one favours ISLA). Protocol: 10,000 sampled surface
#|   points per case, 500 epochs, bfloat16, no augmentation, each architecture
#|   at its best learning rate, three seeds at 35 and 210 cases and two at
#|   1,260, final-epoch checkpoints, validation set; the test split is sealed. The full figure, the
#|   paired per-case statistics, the force-coefficient errors and the controls
#|   are in @sec-data-efficiency. It does not show scaling beyond 1,260 cases
#|   (@sec-limits). Data: results/hilift_ladder_reduction_2026-09-03.json,
#|   results/t1_transolver_control_reduction_2026-09-05.json,
#|   results/w2_reduction_2026-09-07b.json (third seeds).
#| code-fold: true
import json, statistics
from pathlib import Path
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import matplotlib as mpl
BLUE, RED, GREY = "#2a78d6", "#e34948", "#52514e"
INK, INK2, MUTED, GRID, BASELINE = "#0b0b0b", "#52514e", "#898781", "#e1e0d9", "#c3c2b7"
mpl.rcParams.update({"figure.dpi": 110, "font.size": 10, "axes.edgecolor": BASELINE,
                     "axes.labelcolor": INK2, "axes.grid": True, "grid.color": GRID,
                     "xtick.color": MUTED, "ytick.color": MUTED, "xtick.labelcolor": INK2,
                     "ytick.labelcolor": INK2, "axes.spines.top": False,
                     "axes.spines.right": False, "legend.frameon": False})
lad = json.load(open(Path("..") / "results" / "hilift_ladder_reduction_2026-09-03.json"))
t1 = json.load(open(Path("..") / "results" / "t1_transolver_control_reduction_2026-09-05.json"))
w2 = json.load(open(Path("..") / "results" / "w2_reduction_2026-09-07b.json"))["runs"]
lad = {**lad, **{k: v for k, v in w2.items() if k.startswith("lad_hl_")}}
t1 = {**t1, **{k: v for k, v in w2.items() if k.startswith("t1_hl_transolver")}}
rungs = [(35, "lad_hl_{a}_super_scarce_seed{s}"), (210, "lad_hl_{a}_scarce_seed{s}"), (1260, "{a}_hl_lr1_seed{s}")]
data = {}
for arch in ("gt", "mt2"):
    xs, means, lo, hi = [], [], [], []
    for n, pat in rungs:
        v = [lad[pat.format(a=arch, s=s)]["pressure_l2"] for s in (42, 43, 44) if pat.format(a=arch, s=s) in lad]
        xs.append(n); means.append(statistics.mean(v)); lo.append(min(v)); hi.append(max(v))
    data[arch] = (xs, means, lo, hi)
xs, means, lo, hi = [], [], [], []
for n, pat in [(35, "t1_hl_transolver_super_scarce_{lr}_seed{s}"), (210, "t1_hl_transolver_scarce_{lr}_seed{s}")]:
    best = None
    for lr in ("lr1e3", "lr3e3"):
        v = [t1[pat.format(lr=lr, s=s)]["pressure_l2"] for s in (42, 43, 44) if pat.format(lr=lr, s=s) in t1]
        if len(v) >= 2 and (best is None or statistics.mean(v) < statistics.mean(best)):
            best = v
    xs.append(n); means.append(statistics.mean(best)); lo.append(min(best)); hi.append(max(best))
data["t"] = (xs, means, lo, hi)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8.0, 4.8))
style = {"gt": (RED, "GeoTransolver", "o", "-", 2.2), "t": (GREY, "Transolver", "^", "--", 1.6), "mt2": (BLUE, "ISLA", "s", "-", 2.2)}
for arch in ("gt", "t", "mt2"):
    xs, means, lo, hi = data[arch]; c, name, mk, ls, lw = style[arch]
    ax.fill_between(xs, lo, hi, color=c, alpha=0.18, lw=0)
    ax.plot(xs, means, color=c, lw=lw, ls=ls, marker=mk, ms=7, zorder=3)
ax.annotate("GeoTransolver", (35, data["gt"][1][0]), xytext=(14, 2), textcoords="offset points", color=RED, fontweight="bold", va="center")
ax.annotate("ISLA", (210, data["mt2"][1][1]), xytext=(14, -14), textcoords="offset points", color=BLUE, fontweight="bold", va="center")
xm, ym = (35 * 210) ** 0.5, (data["t"][1][0] * data["t"][1][1]) ** 0.5
ax.annotate("Transolver", (xm, ym), xytext=(-3, -7), textcoords="offset points", color=GREY, fontsize=9.5, ha="right", va="top",
            bbox=dict(boxstyle="round,pad=0.15", fc="white", ec="none", alpha=0.85))
for i, n in enumerate((35, 210)):
    r_gt = data["gt"][1][i] / data["mt2"][1][i]; r_t = data["t"][1][i] / data["mt2"][1][i]
    ymid = (data["gt"][1][i] * data["mt2"][1][i]) ** 0.5
    ax.annotate("", (n, data["mt2"][1][i]), (n, data["gt"][1][i]), arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="<->", color=INK2, lw=0.9, shrinkA=4, shrinkB=4))
    ax.text(n * 1.08, ymid, f"GeoTransolver {r_gt:.1f}x ISLA\nTransolver {r_t:.1f}x ISLA", color=INK2, fontsize=9, va="center", linespacing=1.3,
            bbox=dict(boxstyle="round,pad=0.15", fc="white", ec="none", alpha=0.85))
r_full = data["gt"][1][2] / data["mt2"][1][2]
ax.annotate(f"{r_full:.2f}x (parity)", (1260, (data["gt"][1][2] * data["mt2"][1][2]) ** 0.5), xytext=(14, 30), textcoords="offset points", color=INK2, fontsize=9, va="bottom")
ax.set_xscale("log"); ax.set_yscale("log")
ax.set_xticks([35, 210, 1260]); ax.set_xticklabels(["35", "210", "1,260"])
ax.set_yticks([0.04, 0.06, 0.1, 0.2, 0.4]); ax.set_yticklabels(["0.04", "0.06", "0.10", "0.20", "0.40"])
ax.set_xlim(22, 3200)
ax.set_xlabel("Training cases [count]", color=INK2)
ax.set_ylabel("Surface pressure error, rel-L2 [–]", color=INK2)
ax.set_title("Data efficiency on HiLiftAeroML (shared 180-case validation set)", color=INK, loc="left", fontsize=11, pad=10)
ax.grid(True, which="major", color=GRID); ax.grid(False, which="minor")
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

## How to read this book

Part I defines the problem, the datasets and splits, the metrics and the
protocol (@sec-problem), then the architecture, ISLA
(@sec-mt2), and the baselines with the fair-comparison rules
(@sec-baselines). Part II is the evidence on production aerodynamics: data
efficiency (@sec-data-efficiency), accuracy at full data and the robustness
contracts (@sec-full-data), regime extrapolation (@sec-regime-extrapolation),
and boundary-to-interior prediction (@sec-interior), which also answers why
the architecture does not evaluate exact boundary-integral kernels
(@sec-interior-negatives). Part III
states the limits of every claim and the experiments that would move them
(@sec-limits) and holds the live status ledger of the program
(@sec-program-status). The appendix is the dated lab notebook
(@sec-notebook): every preregistration, launch and verdict, including the
failed ones, in the order they happened.

Three habits of this book: a comparison is only reported when parameters,
tokens per case, epochs and peak memory are matched or the mismatch is
stated in the same sentence, and every ratio between architectures is written
as baseline error divided by ISLA error, so a value above one favours ISLA; a claim is only reported with the split it was
measured on and the statistic behind it; and a limit is stated next to the
claim it limits, not in a separate place.

## What this book does not claim

ISLA's data-efficiency advantage is a statement about 35 to 1,260 training
cases on HiLiftAeroML; on DrivAerML, at the frozen learning rate, GeoTransolver
is 1.2–1.3x more accurate from 27 cases up and the two tie at 14. ISLA's curve
flattens where GeoTransolver's steepens: a naive power-law extrapolation of the
two curves puts GeoTransolver at 0.015 and ISLA at 0.029 at 5,000 cases, a
factor of two in GeoTransolver's favour (@sec-limits). The HiLift accuracy
figures are validation-set figures (final-epoch checkpoints, no checkpoint
selection; the sealed test was spent on regime extrapolation). The advantage is geometry generalization — at a
fixed angle of attack on 18 never-seen geometries ISLA is 5.0x more accurate
than GeoTransolver — but the ingredient that carries it is not identified: no
single ISLA ingredient accounts for more than 16% of it (@sec-mechanism). ISLA's exact equivariance is a contract, not an
in-distribution accuracy edge on vehicle data: GeoTransolver trained in a
canonical frame is exactly pose-invariant at 1% cost (@sec-pose). Neither
architecture generalizes across a flow-regime boundary, and neither
transfers zero-shot to a different vehicle family
(@sec-regime-extrapolation, @sec-full-data).
